summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity gives an even representative \(x\) with \(x^2\equiv5\pmod p\); taking \(n=x-1\) factors the continued-fraction numerator as \(n^2+2n-4=x^2-5=pq\), where the proof arranges that the odd cofactor \(q\) is small enough to divide the accompanying denominator. A recurrence invariant shows that \(p\) cannot also divide that denominator (otherwise \(p\mid44\), forcing the separately evaluated case \(p=11\)), so reduction cancels \(q\) but leaves exactly \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
with
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
If the rational number \(R_2(n)\), in lowest terms, is \(N/D\), then \(C_n=D/N\), so the reduced denominator of \(C_n\) is \(|N|\). We shall prove that for the index we construct, the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is the prescribed prime \(p\).

We first develop the integer recurrence underlying \(R_2(n)\).

For a fixed \(n\ge 3\), define integer pairs \((U_t,V_t)\) for \(0\le t\le n-3\) by
\[
(U_0,V_0)=(5n-4,4)
\]
and, for \(t<n-3\),
\[
(U_{t+1},V_{t+1})= igl(kU_t-(k+1)V_t,\,U_t\bigr),
\qquad k=n-2-t.
\]
The initial pair comes from
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=n-1+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}.
\]
An immediate induction on \(t\), using the defining recursion for the continued fraction, gives
\[
R_{n-1-t}(n)=\frac{U_t}{V_t}. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, this is true at \(t=0\), and if it is true at \(t\), then
\[
R_{n-2-t}(n)
=(n-2-t)-\frac{n-1-t}{R_{n-1-t}(n)}
=\frac{(n-2-t)U_t-(n-1-t)V_t}{U_t},
\]
which is precisely \(U_{t+1}/V_{t+1}\).

The pairs satisfy the following invariant:
\[
(K-1)U_t-K(K-2)V_t=n^2+2n-4,
\qquad K=n-1-t. \tag{2}
\]
For \(t=0\), this says
\[
(n-2)(5n-4)-4(n-1)(n-3)=n^2+2n-4,
\]
which follows by expansion. If (2) holds at one step, substitution of
\[
U_{t+1}=(K-1)U_t-KV_t,\qquad V_{t+1}=U_t,
\]
and replacement of \(K\) by \(K-1\) proves the same identity at the next step. Thus (2) holds throughout.

All the integers \(U_t,V_t\) in this range are positive. This is clear initially. At a subsequent step, \(V_{t+1}=U_t>0\). Also, at that step the new value \(K'=n-1-(t+1)\) is at least \(2\), and (2) gives
\[
(K'-1)U_{t+1}
=n^2+2n-4+K'(K'-2)V_{t+1}>0.
\]
Hence \(U_{t+1}>0\) as well.

At the final step \(t=n-3\), we have \(K=2\), so (2) reduces to
\[
U_{n-3}=n^2+2n-4. \tag{3}
\]
Write
\[
F=n^2+2n-4,
\qquad D=V_{n-3}.
\]
Then (1) and (3) give
\[
R_2(n)=\frac FD, \tag{4}
\]
where \(D>0\). The fraction in (4) is not asserted to be reduced; controlling its cancellation is the central point of the proof.

For that purpose, reverse the sequence of first coordinates by setting
\[
A_j=U_{n-3-j}\qquad(0\le j\le n-3).
\]
Then
\[
A_0=F,\qquad A_1=D,\qquad A_{n-3}=U_0=5n-4. \tag{5}
\]
The recurrence for the pairs, read backwards, becomes
\[
A_j=(j+2)A_{j+1}-(j+3)A_{j+2}
\qquad(j+2\le n-3). \tag{6}
\]

We need two consequences of this recurrence.

First, suppose generally that integers \(A_j\) satisfy (6) up to an endpoint \(m\). Then for every \(j<m\) there is an integer \(z_j\) such that
\[
(j+1)!A_j=2jA_1+A_0z_j. \tag{7}
\]
This is proved by a two-step induction. For \(j=0\), take \(z_0=1\), since \(1!A_0=A_0\). For \(j=1\), take \(z_1=0\), since \(2!A_1=2A_1\). Now suppose (7) is known at \(j\) and \(j+1\). From (6),
\[
(j+3)A_{j+2}=(j+2)A_{j+1}-A_j.
\]
Multiplying by \((j+2)!\), and substituting the two induction hypotheses, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(j+3)!A_{j+2}
&=(j+2)(j+2)!A_{j+1}-(j+2)!A_j\\
&=(j+2)\bigl(2(j+1)A_1+A_0z_{j+1}\bigr)
 -(j+2)\bigl(2jA_1+A_0z_j\bigr)\\
&=2(j+2)A_1+A_0\,(j+2)(z_{j+1}-z_j),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (7) at \(j+2\).

Apply this with \(m=n-3\). Let \(q\) be a positive odd integer such that
\[
q\le n-3\quad\text{and}\quad q\mid F.
\]
Use (7) with \(j=q-1\). Since \(q-1<n-3\), it yields
\[
q!A_{q-1}=2(q-1)D+Fz
\]
for some integer \(z\). The left side is divisible by \(q\), because \(q\mid q!\), and \(Fz\) is divisible by \(q\). Therefore
\[
q\mid 2(q-1)D.
\]
Of course \(q\mid 2qD\), and subtracting gives \(q\mid 2D\). Since \(q\) is odd, it is coprime to \(2\), and hence
\[
q\mid D. \tag{8}
\]
This is the first consequence: every sufficiently small odd divisor \(q\) of \(F\) must cancel from the numerator in (4).

The second consequence prevents a sufficiently large prime divisor from canceling. Let \(p\) be a prime satisfying
\[
n<p,\qquad p\ge 11,\qquad p\ne 11,
\]
and suppose \(p\mid F\). We claim
\[
p\nmid D. \tag{9}
\]
Suppose instead that \(p\mid D\). By (5), \(p\mid A_0\) and \(p\mid A_1\). We show inductively that \(p\mid A_j\) for every \(0\le j\le n-3\). If \(p\mid A_j\) and \(p\mid A_{j+1}\), equation (6) implies
\[
p\mid (j+3)A_{j+2}.
\]
Here
\[
0<j+3\le n-2<p,
\]
so the prime \(p\) cannot divide \(j+3\). It follows that \(p\mid A_{j+2}\), completing the induction. In particular, by (5),
\[
p\mid A_{n-3}=5n-4.
\]
We already have \(p\mid F=n^2+2n-4\). Consequently \(p\) divides the integer linear combination
\[
25F-(5n+14)(5n-4)=-44.
\]
Thus \(p\mid44=4\cdot11\). Since \(p\ge11\) is prime, this forces \(p=11\), contrary to the assumption. This proves (9).

We now construct the desired index from the congruence condition on \(p\).

Let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\pmod {10}\quad\text{or}\quad p\equiv9\pmod {10}.
\]
Such a prime is at least \(11\). Moreover, \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Indeed, quadratic reciprocity applies because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), and gives
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
If \(p\equiv1\pmod {10}\), then \(p\equiv1\pmod5\), which is a square modulo \(5\). If \(p\equiv9\pmod {10}\), then \(p\equiv4\pmod5\), which is also a square modulo \(5\). Hence in either case there exists a residue \(r\), with \(0\le r<p\), such that
\[
r^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, exactly one of \(r\) and \(p-r\) is even (unless \(r=0\), which in fact cannot occur here). Choose the even one and call it \(x\). Then
\[
0\le x<p,\qquad x\text{ is even},\qquad x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{10}
\]
In fact \(x\ge4\). If the nonnegative even integer \(x\) were at most \(2\), then \(x^2\) and \(5\) would both lie between \(0\) and \(p-1\), since \(p\ge11\). Their congruence modulo \(p\) would force \(x^2=5\), impossible.

We first treat the exceptional prime \(p=11\). Taking \(n=3\),
\[
R_2(3)=2+\frac34=\frac{11}{4},
\]
so the original continued fraction is \(4/11\), whose denominator is \(11\). Thus \(a(3)=11\).

Assume from now on that \(p\ne11\). Then the even root \(x\) in (10) cannot equal \(4\), because \(x=4\) would give
\[
p\mid x^2-5=11,
\]
and, as \(p\ge11\) is prime, this would imply \(p=11\). Therefore
\[
6\le x<p. \tag{11}
\]
Since \(p\mid x^2-5\), define the positive integer
\[
q=\frac{x^2-5}{p}.
\]
Thus
\[
pq=x^2-5. \tag{12}
\]
It is positive because \(x\ge6\). It is also odd: \(x\) is even, so \(x^2-5\) is odd; since \(p\) is odd and \(pq=x^2-5\), \(q\) must be odd.

We next prove the important size bound
\[
q\le x-4. \tag{13}
\]
First, \(q<x\). Otherwise, using \(p>x\), we would have
\[
pq\ge (x+1)x>x^2-5,
\]
contradicting (12). Since \(q\) is odd and \(x\) is even, if (13) failed then the only possibilities between \(x-3\) and \(x-1\) would be
\[
q=x-3\quad\text{or}\quad q=x-1.
\]
If \(q=x-1\), then \(x=q+1\), while \(p>x\) implies \(p\ge q+2\). Equation (12) would give
\[
pq=(q+1)^2-5=q^2+2q-4,
\]
but \(p\ge q+2\) gives \(pq\ge q^2+2q\), a contradiction.

If \(q=x-3\), then \(x=q+3\), and (12) gives
\[
pq=(q+3)^2-5=q^2+6q+4,
\]
so
\[
q(p-q-6)=4.
\]
In particular, the positive odd integer \(q\) divides \(4\), hence \(q=1\). Then \(x=q+3=4\), and (12) yields \(p=11\), again a contradiction. Thus (13) is proved.

Now set
\[
n=x-1.
\]
By (11), \(n\ge5\), and because \(x<p\), we have \(n<p\). Furthermore,
\[
F=n^2+2n-4=(x-1)^2+2(x-1)-4=x^2-5=pq. \tag{14}
\]
Also, (13) becomes
\[
q\le x-4=n-3. \tag{15}
\]
The integer \(q\) is positive and odd, divides \(F\), and satisfies (15). Therefore the first recurrence consequence, equation (8), applies and shows that \(q\mid D\). Write
\[
D=qd
\]
with \(d>0\); positivity follows from \(D>0\) and \(q>0\).

On the other hand, \(p\mid F\), \(n<p\), \(p\ge11\), and \(p\ne11\). The second recurrence consequence, equation (9), therefore gives \(p\nmid D\). Since \(d\mid D\), it follows that \(p\nmid d\). As \(p\) is prime, this means
\[
\gcd(p,d)=1. \tag{16}
\]

Finally, substituting (14) and \(D=qd\) into (4), we obtain
\[
R_2(n)=\frac{F}{D}=\frac{pq}{qd}=\frac pd.
\]
By (16), this is already in lowest terms, and both \(p\) and \(d\) are positive. Thus the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is exactly \(p\). Consequently the reciprocal continued fraction \(C_n=1/R_2(n)\) has reduced denominator \(p\), so
\[
a(n)=p.
\]

For \(p=11\) we found the index \(n=3\), and for every other prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\) modulo \(10\) the construction above gives \(n=x-1\). Hence every prime ending in \(1\) or \(9\) occurs in A363347.
